finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the missing 'dba' role check is never enforced. Any request that reaches the handler as a user can drop tables. Because r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the SQL string, the table name is also an SQL injection vector (for example "x; DELETE FROM users").
finding.source: Any authenticated user without the dba role (or any user the upstream layer places in context) sending POST/GET /admin/drop with form parameter t. The t value is fully attacker-controlled.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered directly with dropTable and no auth middleware
userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the context value
Authorize(u, "dba") returns errors.New("forbidden") for non-dba users, but the return value is discarded
execution continues and attacker-controlled t is concatenated into the DROP TABLE statement

finding.guards_checked: Compared with vacuum (api.go:33-36), which checks the Authorize error and returns 403. dropTable has no equivalent check. No middleware is registered in main (api.go:43-46). There is no validation or allowlist on t. runSQL is a stub here, but it is the SQL sink by name and usage.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: Authorize's error is discarded at api.go:26; no middleware in main (api.go:43-46); no allowlist or parameterization on t. Caveat: nothing in this file sets the "user" context value, so userFrom (api.go:22) would panic on the nil assertion, which means this snippet alone never reaches the sink. The finding holds only if an upstream layer outside this file sets it.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 calls Authorize(u, "dba") as a bare statement and discards the error, unlike vacuum at api.go:33-36, so a non-dba user reaches api.go:27, where the form value t is concatenated into the DROP TABLE statement. This assumes some code outside this file populates the "user" context value, because without it userFrom panics first.

finding.claim: userFrom performs an unchecked type assertion on the request context value. If no upstream middleware sets "user" (and main registers none), the assertion panics for every request. In dropTable, a nil *User would also be dereferenced in Authorize. This is a robustness and availability issue and shows that authentication is not enforced anywhere in this file.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated HTTP client requesting /admin/drop or /admin/vacuum

trace.note: Handlers are registered on the default mux without an authentication middleware
The single-value type assertion panics when the context value is absent. net/http recovers per connection, so the result is a failed request and a logged panic rather than a process crash.

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware exists in the repo, which has only api.go. Panic recovery by net/http limits the impact to a failed request. If an external layer always sets the user, this is not exploitable. This is low severity and depends on deployment.

verdict.guard_found: none (no auth middleware; only net/http's per-connection panic recovery limits impact to a failed request)
verdict.reason: api.go:22 uses a single-value assertion on r.Context().Value("user"), and main (api.go:44-46) registers no middleware to set it, so any anonymous request to /admin/drop or /admin/vacuum panics; net/http recovery makes it a low-severity availability/robustness issue. Related but separate: api.go:26 discards Authorize's result, so dropTable has no authorization check at all if a user is ever set.
